doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thornton
title: Sippie and Big Mama in the dressing room; women pianists and singers
summary: Jeannie recounts the dressing room argument and a singer in Buffalo who doubted a woman pianist.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well we’re working on it. You know Sippie and Big Mama were fighting in the dressing room. And one would sit on that end and one sit — and that’s the one thing that we didn’t know. Now Big Mama is big, she’s got a big feet like this. And Sippie’s got a little tiny feet. So Sippie says, she says, “You know, my granddaughter bought me these shoes. They’re a size four and they’re too big.” So Big Mama says, “I don’t know why you’re complaining, you ought to be glad you’ve got feet.” And so then Sippie said a word that I can’t say on camera. And so it got really blue in there. And I said to myself, Lordy, nobody knows these two ladies aren’t ladies. They’re no longer ladies. I never heard such.
Did you ever, when you had first started to conceive of this program, did you think that that might happen?
No. It never occurred to me. But I forgot that thing, because almost all vocalists, said oh Jeannie, watch it.
Sometimes they don’t like each other and they call each other names behind each other’s back. I don’t know why.
Yeah. They have an ax to grind.
You know I think you have, because you play piano so well, I think it gives you a leg up on your confidence level.
That’s why they do that, because they’re at your mercy.
They are sure at your mercy, that’s right. And you’re not. And I think it makes a big difference.

Remember that one that had the attitude in Buffalo? Came on and decided, “Well I’m not used to having a woman piano player. And I’ve had Hank Jones play for me.” And I said to myself, why is she saying that? So she put her music up there, and so then she started singing “My Funny Valentine.” And so every time she said [sings] “my funny valentine” I moved up a half step. “Sweet funny valentine” another half step. “You made me smile when you’re”— I said now that’ll teach her. And so after that, she had much respect.
You just don’t do that. It’s just like arguing with the waiter, with your food, you know—
Then he’ll go back in the kitchen and decorate it for you. So don’t be messing around.
That should be a book of quotes, you know, the Cheathams say, “Don’t mess with the waiter, and don’t mess with the piano player.”
So she got respect for me.
I like that. My. Well you really should consider a book you know.
Well we’re kind of working on one.
